paragraphs.heading: Rock made from rock
paragraphs.text: Metamorphic rocks come from existing rock that is transformed into a new type of rock, a process called metamorphism. The original rock, called the protolith, is exposed to temperatures above 150 to 200 °C and, often, pressures of 100 megapascals or more. It stays mostly solid throughout, yet it slowly recrystallizes and takes on a new texture or mineral composition. The protolith may be igneous, sedimentary, or an existing metamorphic rock.

paragraphs.heading: Where it happens
paragraphs.text: Metamorphic rocks are one of the three great divisions of rock types. They make up a large part of Earth's crust and form 12% of its land surface. Some form simply by deep burial, where temperatures are high and the rock layers above press down with great pressure. Others form through tectonic processes such as continental collisions, which bring horizontal pressure, friction and distortion. Rock can also be changed locally when it is heated by an intrusion of magma, hot molten rock from Earth's interior.

paragraphs.heading: Chalk in a cannon barrel
paragraphs.text: The importance of heating was first noted by the Scottish naturalist James Hutton. In 1795 he wrote that some rock beds of the Scottish Highlands had started as sedimentary rock and had been transformed by great heat. Hutton also guessed that pressure mattered. His friend James Hall tested the idea by sealing chalk into a makeshift pressure vessel built from a cannon barrel and heating it in an iron foundry furnace. The result strongly resembled marble, not the usual quicklime that chalk gives when heated in open air.

paragraphs.heading: New minerals, same ingredients
paragraphs.text: A rock's minerals can change even when its bulk composition does not. That is possible because each mineral stays stable only inside a certain range of temperature, pressure and chemical surroundings. At atmospheric pressure, for example, the mineral kyanite turns into andalusite at about 190 °C. Andalusite in turn becomes sillimanite at about 800 °C. All three share the identical composition, Al₂SiO₅.

paragraphs.heading: Growing new crystals
paragraphs.text: The change in a rock's particle size during metamorphism is called recrystallization. The small calcite crystals in limestone and chalk, for instance, change into larger crystals in marble. In sandstone, the original quartz sand grains recrystallize into very compact quartzite, whose often larger quartz crystals are interlocked. Both high temperature and high pressure help. Heat lets atoms and ions in solid crystals migrate and reorganize the crystals, while pressure causes crystals to dissolve where they touch one another.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the record
paragraphs.text: Because each mineral is stable only within certain limits, finding certain minerals in a metamorphic rock shows roughly the temperatures and pressures at which it was changed. These are known as index minerals. Metamorphic rocks are now exposed at the surface after erosion and uplift, and studying them gives information about the temperatures and pressures deep in Earth's crust.

paragraphs.heading: Familiar examples
paragraphs.text: Gneiss, slate, marble, schist and quartzite are all metamorphic rocks. Slate and quartzite tiles are used in building, and marble is prized for building and as a medium for sculpture. Schist bedrock, on the other hand, has pronounced planes of weakness, which can make it a challenge for civil engineering.
